title: Detecting Initial System-Environment Correlations from a Single Observable
comment: The manuscript is 12 pages long and includes 5 figures. Comments are welcome
summary:
We address the problem of detecting initial system--environment correlations when the environment is not directly accessible. Most existing approaches rely on full state tomography or multiple system preparations, which can be experimentally demanding.
  We show that, for a known interaction, it can be sufficient to monitor a single expectation value of the system. Focusing on a qubit interacting with an environment via isotropic Heisenberg exchange, we derive exact bounds on the signal $z(t)=\langleσ_z^S\rangle(t)$ that hold for all factorized initial states. These bounds define a \emph{factorized envelope}: if an observed trajectory exits this envelope at any time, initial system--environment correlations are certified.
  From a reduced-dynamics perspective, the envelope admits a clear operational interpretation as the admissible region generated by the standard product assignment (embedding) map, which serves as a null model for uncorrelated preparations. Envelope violations therefore rule out the entire product-assignment class using only a single calibrated observable.
  We illustrate the method using three families of correlated initial states and observe clear envelope violations, including cases in which the reduced system state is maximally mixed. We further show that the same single-observable logic extends to an exactly solvable pure-dephasing spin--boson model with an infinite environment, where factorized initial states generate a simple coherence envelope whose violation certifies initial correlations. Overall, our results demonstrate that single-axis measurements, combined with a one-time calibration of $ρ_S(0)$, can certify initial system--environment correlations without tomography or environment access.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a method to detect initial system-environment correlations using a single observable instead of requiring full state tomography or multiple preparations, specifically focusing on a qubit with isotropic Heisenberg exchange interaction.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for detecting correlations are often experimentally demanding due to the need for full state tomography or multiple system preparations. This paper seeks a more efficient method.
AI.method: The authors derive exact bounds on the signal related to the qubit's observable, establishing a 'factorized envelope.' If this envelope is violated, it indicates the presence of initial correlations. The method is operationally interpreted within a reduced-dynamics framework, allowing certification using only one calibrated observable.
AI.result: The method correctly detected envelope violations for various correlated initial states, even in scenarios where the reduced system state was maximally mixed. It also extends to a pure-dephasing spin-boson model, demonstrating broader applicability.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that monitoring a single expectation value can effectively certify initial system-environment correlations without the need for extensive experimental setups.

title: Why measurements are made of effects
summary: Both in quantum theory and in general probabilistic theories, measurements with $n$ outcomes are modelled as $n$-tuples of \emph{effects} summing up to the unit effect. Why is this the case, and can this assumption be meaningfully relaxed? Here we develop \emph{generalized measurement theories (GMTs)} as a mathematical framework for physical theories that is complementary to general probabilistic theories, and where this kind of question can be made precise and answered. We then give a definition of \emph{probabilistic state} on a GMT, prove that measurements are made of effects in every GMT in which the probabilistic states separate the measurements, and also argue that this separation condition is physically well-motivated. Finally, we also discuss when a GMT should be considered classical and characterize GMTs corresponding to Boolean algebras as those that are strongly classical and projective.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the nature of measurements in quantum and probabilistic theories, proposes a framework for generalized measurement theories (GMTs), and defines key concepts within this framework.
AI.motivation: The study investigates why measurements with multiple outcomes are structured as sums of effects equating to a unit effect, and examines whether this structure can be relaxed.
AI.method: The authors develop generalized measurement theories (GMTs) to provide a formal framework for exploring these measurement questions and define the notion of a probabilistic state within this context.
AI.result: The paper proves that measurements are comprised of effects in every GMT where probabilistic states effectively separate the measurements, supporting the separation condition as both mathematically robust and physically relevant.
AI.conclusion: The authors classify GMTs related to Boolean algebras as strongly classical and projective, outlining conditions under which a GMT can be deemed classical.

title: Trotter Error and Orbital Transformations in Quantum Phase Estimation
summary: Quantum computation with Trotter product formulae is straightforward and requires little overhead in terms of logical qubits. The choice of the orbital basis significantly affects circuit depth, with localised orbitals yielding lowest circuit depths. However, literature results point to large Trotter errors incurred by localised orbitals. Here, we therefore investigate the effect of orbital transformations on Trotter error. We consider three strategies to reduce Trotter error by orbital transformation: (i) The a priori selection of an orbital basis that produces low Trotter error. (ii) The derivation of an orbital basis that produces a ground state energy free of Trotter error (as we observed that the Trotter error is a continuous function in the Givens-rotation parameter, from which continuity of this error upon orbital transformation can be deduced). (iii) Application of propagators that change the computational basis between Trotter steps. Our numerical results show that reliably reducing Trotter error by orbital transformations is challenging. General recipes to produce low Trotter errors cannot be easily derived, despite analytical expressions which suggest ways to decrease Trotter error. Importantly, we found that localised orbital bases do not produce large Trotter errors in molecular calculations, which is an important result for efficient QPE set-ups.

AI.tldr: This study explores the impact of orbital transformations on Trotter error in quantum computation, highlighting the challenges in reducing this error despite some promising strategies.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the significant Trotter errors associated with localised orbital bases in quantum computations using Trotter product formulae, which affects circuit efficiency.
AI.method: The study investigates three strategies for reducing Trotter error through orbital transformations: (i) pre-selecting an optimal orbital basis, (ii) deriving an orbital basis that eliminates Trotter error for ground state energy, and (iii) utilizing propagators to change computational basis during Trotter steps.
AI.result: Numerical results reveal that effectively reducing Trotter error via orbital transformations is complex, with no general recipes available, though localised orbitals do not yield substantial errors in molecular calculations.
AI.conclusion: The findings underscore the practicality of using localised orbitals in quantum phase estimation setups, despite the theoretical expectations of Trotter errors.

title: Near-perfect Noisy Quantum State Teleportation
summary: Achieving high fidelity of quantum teleportation (QT) in a noisy environment is an essential requirement for its real-world applications. To this end, we devise a distinctive protocol for ensuring teleportation fidelity {\it close to unity}, hinging essentially on the timing of Alice's Bell-basis measurement (BM) dependent on the choice of Bob's local noise parameters, but is independent of Alice's local noise. Our scheme is enabled by Alice communicating to Bob only two of the BM outcomes corresponding to the states that are decoherence-free under common dephasing at Alice's wing. On the other hand, Bob is asked to discard the states of his qubit for the other two BM outcomes in order to maximize fidelity of the teleported state. This ensures the teleportation fidelity's independence of noise parameters in Alice's wing. We formulate the protocol in terms of a generic two-level quantum system, subjected to non-Markovian dephasing noise, applicable for any pure maximally/non-maximally entangled state as well as a Werner-type mixed state as resource. Notably, we show that high fidelity is achievable even using resource states with small values of the entanglement measure. Remarkably, even within the local regime of Werner states, where Bell-CHSH inequalities are not violated, the teleportation fidelity remains significantly high. Finally, we discuss the empirical feasibility of our scheme using photonic qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unique protocol for enhancing quantum teleportation fidelity in noisy environments by optimizing measurement timing and selectively discarding certain outcomes.
AI.motivation: To achieve high fidelity in quantum teleportation despite noise, which is crucial for practical applications.
AI.method: The protocol depends on Alice's Bell-basis measurement timing, which is informed by Bob's local noise parameters. Alice communicates specific results to Bob to focus on decoherence-free states, leading to the discarding of less optimal states for higher fidelity.
AI.result: The protocol maintains high teleportation fidelity even for resource states with low entanglement, and works effectively under non-Markovian dephasing noise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme is feasible using photonic qubits and demonstrates resilience against local noise, providing a pathway for practical quantum teleportation.

title: Eigenstate-assisted realization of general quantum controlled unitaries with a fixed cost
summary: Controlled unitary gates are a basic element in many quantum algorithms. Converting a general unitary $U$ with a known decomposition into its controlled version, controlled-$U$, can introduce a large overhead in terms of the depth of the circuit. We present a general method to take any unitary $U$ into controlled-$U$ using a fixed circuit with 4 CNOT gates and 2 Toffoli gates per qubit. For $n$-qubit unitaries and one control qubit, we require $2n+1$ qubits and a circuit that can generate an eigenstate of $U$, for which there are many cost-effective known algorithms. The method also works for any black block implementation of $U$, achieving a constant-depth realization independent of its decomposition. We illustrate its use in the Hadamard test and discuss applications to variational and quantum machine-learning algorithms.

AI.tldr: A method is presented to convert any unitary $U$ into its controlled version, controlled-$U$, using a fixed circuit with minimal qubit requirements.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of significant overhead in circuit depth when converting unitary operations to their controlled versions in quantum algorithms.
AI.method: The proposed method utilizes a circuit consisting of 4 CNOT gates and 2 Toffoli gates per qubit, requiring $2n+1$ qubits for $n$-qubit unitaries with one control qubit.
AI.result: This method ensures constant-depth realization of controlled unitaries, independent of the specific decomposition of $U$, and can be applied to black block implementations as well.
AI.conclusion: The technique's application extends to the Hadamard test and various algorithms in variational and quantum machine learning.

title: Contextuality-enhanced quantum state discrimination under fixed failure probability
summary: Quantum state discrimination enables the accurate identification of quantum states, which are generally nonorthogonal. Among various strategies, minimum-error discrimination and unambiguous state discrimination exhibit contextuality-enhanced success probabilities that surpass classical bounds, offering significant advantages for quantum sensing and communication. However, in practice, both error and failure outcomes can occur, suggesting the need for a unified strategy that incorporates both aspects while exploring the potential for contextuality enhancement. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate contextuality enhancement in quantum state discrimination under a fixed failure probability. We show that this enhancement disappears within a certain intermediate range of failure probabilities--a phenomenon absent in conventional strategies, where both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination consistently outperform the noncontextual bound for equal priors. Moreover, we analyze how the existence of this non-enhancement region depends on the confusability of the quantum states, which corresponds to their fidelity in a quantum model. We further extend the discussion to the noisy state discrimination, which even encompasses the maximal-confidence discrimination. In this extended discussion, we observe that the non-enhancement region tends to disappear with increasing noise strength.

AI.tldr: This work theoretically shows that contextuality enhancement in quantum state discrimination persists under fixed failure probabilities but vanishes at intermediate failure rates, differing from conventional strategies that ensure consistent outperformance.
AI.motivation: To address the need for a unified quantum state discrimination strategy that accounts for both error and failure outcomes while enhancing contextuality.
AI.method: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of contextuality enhancement in quantum state discrimination models, evaluating how this enhancement is affected by fixed failure probabilities and the confusability of quantum states.
AI.result: Contextuality enhancement is demonstrated theoretically, but it disappears within an intermediate failure probability range, a unique finding not observed in classical strategies that outperform noncontextual bounds.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals a non-enhancement region linked to the confusability of quantum states and shows that increasing noise strength tends to eliminate this region.

title: Quantum Hamiltonian Learning using Time-Resolved Measurement Data and its Application to Gene Regulatory Network Inference
summary: We present a new Hamiltonian-learning framework based on time-resolved measurement data from a fixed local IC-POVM and its application to inferring gene regulatory networks. We introduce the quantum Hamiltonian-based gene-expression model (QHGM), in which gene interactions are encoded as a parameterized Hamiltonian that governs gene expression evolution over pseudotime. We derive finite-sample recovery guarantees and establish upper bounds on the number of time and measurement samples required for accurate parameter estimation with high probability, scaling polynomially with system size. To recover the QHGM parameters, we develop a scalable variational learning algorithm based on empirical risk minimization. Our method recovers network structure efficiently on synthetic benchmarks and reveals novel, biologically plausible regulatory connections in Glioblastoma single-cell RNA sequencing data, highlighting its potential in cancer research. This framework opens new directions for applying quantum-like modeling to biological systems beyond the limits of classical inference.

AI.tldr: A new framework for Hamiltonian learning leverages quantum models for gene regulatory networks, demonstrating efficient parameter recovery with potential applications in cancer research.
AI.motivation: To infer gene regulatory networks using quantum Hamiltonian models, addressing limitations in classical inference methods.
AI.method: Introduced QHGM with time-resolved measurements from a fixed local IC-POVM; derived recovery guarantees and bounds; developed a scalable variational learning algorithm based on empirical risk minimization.
AI.result: Efficiently recovers network structure on synthetic benchmarks and identifies novel regulatory connections in Glioblastoma RNA sequencing data.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables quantum-like modeling in biological systems, indicating its potential for advancing cancer research beyond classical approaches.

title: A Relation Between the Chrestenson Operator, Weyl Operator Basis, and Kronecker-Pauli Operator Basis
summary: Within the framework of quantum theory, we review the Chrestenson operator, the Weyl operator basis, and the Kronecker-Pauli operator basis in $d$-dimensional Hilbert spaces using Dirac notation, where $d$ is a prime integer strictly greater than 2. We establish a new algebraic relation connecting these operators and present the cases $d=3$ and $d=5$ as illustrative examples.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews key quantum operators in $d$-dimensional Hilbert spaces and establishes a novel algebraic relation between them.
AI.motivation: To explore the connections among different operator bases within quantum theory in higher-dimensional spaces.
AI.method: The authors utilize Dirac notation to analyze the Chrestenson operator, Weyl operator basis, and Kronecker-Pauli operator basis for prime dimensions greater than 2.
AI.result: A new algebraic relation is established between the aforementioned operators, with specific cases demonstrated for $d=3$ and $d=5$.
AI.conclusion: The findings enhance the understanding of operator relationships in quantum mechanics, particularly in higher-dimensional systems.

title: Magnon squeezing in the quantum regime
summary: Squeezed states, crucial for quantum metrology and emerging quantum technologies, have been demonstrated in various platforms, but quantum squeezing of magnons in macroscopic spin systems remains elusive. Here we report the experimental observation of quantum-level magnon squeezing in a millimeter-scale yttrium iron garnet (YIG) sphere. By engineering a strong dispersive magnon-superconducting qubit coupling via a microwave cavity, we implement a significant self-Kerr nonlinearity to generate squeezed magnon states with their mean magnon number less than one. Harnessing a magnon-assisted Raman process, we perform Wigner tomography, revealing quadrature variances of $\sim\!0.8$ ($\sim\!1.0$~dB squeezing) relative to the vacuum. These results lay the groundwork for quantum nonlinear magnonics and promise potential applications in quantum metrology.

AI.tldr: This study presents the first observation of quantum-level magnon squeezing in a YIG sphere, utilizing magnon-superconducting qubit coupling and revealing significant implications for quantum technologies.
AI.motivation: There is a need for quantum squeezing of magnons in macroscopic spin systems to enhance quantum metrology and develop new quantum technologies.
AI.method: The authors engineer a strong dispersive coupling between magnons and a superconducting qubit through a microwave cavity, implementing self-Kerr nonlinearity to produce squeezed magnon states with a mean magnon number below one, and use magnon-assisted Raman processes for Wigner tomography.
AI.result: The experiments demonstrate quadrature variances of ~0.8, indicating ~1.0 dB of squeezing relative to the vacuum, marking a significant achievement in the field.
AI.conclusion: The findings advance the development of quantum nonlinear magnonics and highlight their potential applications in quantum metrology.

title: Improving Generalization and Trainability of Quantum Eigensolvers via Graph Neural Encoding
summary: Determining the ground state of a many-body Hamiltonian is a central problem across physics, chemistry, and combinatorial optimization, yet it is often classically intractable due to the exponential growth of Hilbert space with system size. Even on fault-tolerant quantum computers, quantum algorithms with convergence guarantees -- such as quantum phase estimation and quantum subspace methods -- require an initial state with sufficiently large overlap with the true ground state to be effective. Variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) are natural candidates for preparing such states; however, standard VQEs typically exhibit poor generalization, requiring retraining for each Hamiltonian instance, and often suffer from barren plateaus, where gradients can vanish exponentially with circuit depth and system size. To address these limitations, we propose an end-to-end representation learning framework that combines a graph autoencoder with a classical neural network to generate VQE parameters that generalize across Hamiltonian instances. By encoding interaction topology and coupling structure, the proposed model produces high-overlap initial states without instance-specific optimization. Through extensive numerical experiments on families of one- and two-local Hamiltonians, we demonstrate improved generalization and trainability, manifested as reduced test error and a significantly milder decay of gradient variance. We further show that our method substantially accelerates convergence in quantum subspace-based eigensolvers, highlighting its practical impact for downstream quantum algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel framework combining graph autoencoders and neural networks to enhance the performance of Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) in finding ground states of many-body Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: The challenge of determining the ground state of many-body Hamiltonians is critical in various fields but is compounded by classical intractability and inefficiencies in existing quantum methods.
AI.method: The proposed method integrates a graph autoencoder with a classical neural network to generate VQE parameters that effectively generalize across different Hamiltonian instances, encoding interaction and coupling structures.
AI.result: Numerical experiments demonstrate that the framework improves generalization and trainability of VQEs, leading to reduced test errors and better gradient stability, as well as accelerated convergence in quantum eigensolvers.
AI.conclusion: The approach significantly enhances the practical usability of quantum algorithms by producing high-overlap initial states and mitigating issues faced by standard VQEs.

title: Unlocking photodetection for quantum sensing with Bayesian likelihood-free methods and deep learning
summary: To operate quantum sensors at their quantum limit in real time, it is crucial to identify efficient data inference tools for rapid parameter estimation. In photodetection, the key challenge is the fast interpretation of click-patterns that exhibit non-classical statistics -- the very features responsible for the quantum enhancement of precision. We achieve this goal by comparing Bayesian likelihood-free methods with ones based on deep learning (DL). While the former are more conceptually intuitive, the latter, once trained, provide significantly faster estimates with comparable precision and yield similar predictions of the associated errors, challenging a common misconception that DL lacks such capabilities. We first verify both approaches for an analytically tractable, yet multiparameter, scenario of a two-level system emitting uncorrelated photons. Our main result, however, is the application to a driven nonlinear optomechanical device emitting non-classical light with complex multiclick correlations; in this case, our methods are essential for fast inference and, hence, unlock the possibility of distinguishing different photon statistics in real time. Our results pave the way for dynamical control of quantum sensors that leverage non-classical effects in photodetection.

AI.tldr: The paper compares Bayesian likelihood-free methods with deep learning for rapid parameter estimation in quantum sensors, finding that deep learning offers faster estimates without sacrificing precision.
AI.motivation: Efficient data inference tools are needed for real-time operation of quantum sensors at the quantum limit, especially for interpreting click-patterns in photodetection.
AI.method: The study compares Bayesian likelihood-free methods with deep learning techniques, verifying results with both approaches on a two-level system and applying them to a nonlinear optomechanical device.
AI.result: Deep learning methods provide faster estimates with comparable precision to Bayesian methods and are effective in real-time distinctions of photon statistics in complex scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the use of deep learning for dynamic control in quantum sensors, enhancing the ability to leverage non-classical effects in photodetection.

title: The quantum superluminality in the tunnel-ionization process of H-like atoms
summary:
The quantum tunneling time remains the subject of heated debate,
  and one of its most curious features is faster-than-light or
  superluminal tunneling.
  Our tunnel-ionization model of the time-delay, presented in previous work, shows good agreement with the attoclock measurement in the adiabatic and nonadiabatic field calibrations, which also enables the determination of the barrier time-delay.
  In the present work, we show that the tunnel-ionization for H-like atoms with large nuclear charge can be superluminal (quantum superluminality), which in principle can be investigated experimentally using the attoclock scheme.
  We discuss the quantum superluminality in detail for the different regimes of the tunnel-ionization. Our result shows that quantum tunneling faster-than-light is indeed possible, albeit only under somewhat extreme conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper explores the concept of superluminal tunneling in quantum mechanics, specifically through a tunnel-ionization model that aligns with attoclock measurements for H-like atoms with high nuclear charge.
AI.motivation: Understanding quantum tunneling and its time dynamics is crucial due to ongoing debates about its implications, including superluminal effects.
AI.method: The authors extend their previous tunnel-ionization model to investigate the conditions under which superluminal tunneling occurs in H-like atoms and relate their findings to attoclock experimental setups.
AI.result: Superluminal tunneling was demonstrated in specific regimes for H-like atoms, indicating that quantum tunneling can occur faster than light under extreme conditions.
AI.conclusion: Quantum superluminality is theoretically possible, opening pathways for experimental verification using attoclock techniques.

title: Quantum simulation in the Heisenberg picture via vectorization
summary: We present a general framework for simulating quantum systems in the Heisenberg picture on quantum hardware. Based on the vectorization map, our framework fully exploits the mapping between operators and quantum states, allowing any task defined on Heisenberg operators to be mapped to standard Schrödinger-picture tasks that are naturally accessible via quantum computers and simulators. This yields new or improved protocols for tasks such as operator sampling, the computation of OTOCs/superoperator expectation values and their higher order moments, two-point correlators, and operator stabilizer and entanglement entropies. Our approach is also amenable to implementation, as it inherits the structure and resource requirements of the (forward and time-reversed) Schrödinger-picture quantum simulation problem. We demonstrate this by proposing implementations of our framework for a 2D problem on digital and analog quantum simulators, taking into account device connectivity constraints.

AI.tldr: A quantum simulation framework utilizing the Heisenberg picture is introduced, enabling various tasks to be executed more efficiently on quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: To provide a robust method for simulating quantum systems that enhances the utility of quantum hardware by leveraging operators represented in the Heisenberg picture.
AI.method: The framework employs the vectorization map to translate Heisenberg operator tasks into tasks suited for the Schrödinger picture, facilitating easier simulation on quantum devices.
AI.result: New and improved protocols for operator sampling, computation of OTOCs, two-point correlators, and entanglement measures are developed, demonstrating efficacy on both digital and analog quantum simulators.
AI.conclusion: Implementation feasibility is confirmed for a 2D quantum problem, accommodating device connectivity constraints and retaining necessary resource structures.
